diagnose:payroll.business: payroll: Quillfield Home Care Staffing, a home health staffing agency with 4 branches (LNF, HPT, BRW, TLS). It also runs payroll for Amberlane Hospice at Kestrel Bend (KSB) as paymaster. The workbook is a 2026 payroll register. Two system exports are stacked: the old one covers checks 01/09 to 04/07/2026 (text dates, LAST, FIRST names, branch names, 5-digit check numbers) and the new one covers 2026-04-17 to 2026-08-21 (real dates, First Last names, branch codes, 70xxxx check numbers). Each export ends in its own total row. Employees and Branches are lookup tabs. The tool picked payroll_hr correctly. The grill asked 7 questions and the build pick. Every judge error traces to 3 things: KSB left in (all models), old-system OT not subtracted, and the mixed-format Check Date.

facts.fact: KSB (Kestrel Bend) is not our branch. Quillfield is paymaster for Amberlane, which reimburses every dollar. Leave KSB out of labor cost, gross, hours, OT and headcount. Older rows name it Kestrel Bend.
facts.question: None. The owner put it in the free text of 'Who counts in headcount? Pick all that apply (part-time, seasonal, 1099 contractors, people on leave)'.
facts.data_signal: Branches have been mapped name-to-code. KSB has 407 of 3,167 rows (12.9%) but 2,229.5 of 3,583 OT hours (62.2%). That is 5.48 OT hrs per row, against 0.44 to 0.56 for the other four branches (about 10x). Its share of gross (16.7%) is also above its share of rows. On the Branches tab, KSB's manager (Hollis Vandermeer) is the only branch manager with no paycheck on the register: the tool's own 'share 80% of values' join is exactly 4 of 5, and the missing 1 is KSB. Employees shows 28 KSB staff (E0298 to E0325). The note that landed reads: 'Headcount includes, per the owner: "Not sure about those groups. Leave out the Kestrel Bend (KSB) Amberlane staff and E0999 Jordan Pell ..."'
facts.root_cause: No detector for this. (1) No scope or ownership question on the entity dimension: the payroll playbook only has the canned headcount_def options. (2) No group-outlier detector comparing metric share with row share. (3) The partial join was asked as 'Are they the same ID?' and never named the one unmatched value. (4) The owner's volunteered leave-out was not turned into a rule. rules.exclusions only reads free text from answers whose kind is in _KINDS={exclusion,scope,coverage}, and headcount_def is kind 'definition'. Rerunning it confirms {} was returned. With kind 'exclusion' the same parser yields Branch in {ksb, kestrel bend} and Emp ID {e0999}. (5) The template 'Headcount includes, per the owner:' framed the exclusion as headcount-only. So there is no counted 'totals without KSB' note, and top_share, spread and count_distinct all keep KSB.
facts.code_refs: playbooks/payroll_hr.json questions.headcount_def (fact.statement 'Headcount includes, per the owner: {answer_labels}'); sheetbrain/rules.py _KINDS and exclusions(); sheetbrain/interview.py _bridge_questions() prompt text; sheetbrain/analyze.py _table_insights() (no share-vs-rows outlier check); sheetbrain/brain.py Composer._exclusion_facts() (never fires because excluded==[])
facts.general_fix: (a) A data-grounded scope question for the main table's entity dimension (location, department, client, entity). List each value with its row share and metric share, and offer: all ours / some are run for someone else or pass-through (leave out) / some are closed or tests (leave out) / not sure. Leave-out picks carry meta.exclude. (b) A group-outlier finding: for each additive metric x entity, flag a group whose metric share / row share is more than 3x the median of the other groups. Name the numbers and offer a 'not ours, leave out' option. (c) For a partial join from a lookup column, name the unmatched lookup rows and their other attributes. Never ask 'same ID?' about name columns. (d) Run the leave-out parser on every free-text answer, whatever the question kind. When it names values the data holds, write an exclusion record and ask one scope follow-up: 'Leave these out of every total, or only headcount?'

facts.fact: The Branch column holds names on old-system rows (Linden Falls ... Kestrel Bend) and codes on new-system rows (LNF ... KSB). Names must be mapped to codes before any branch total.
facts.question: None
facts.data_signal: Register Branch has 10 distinct values. They are exactly the 5 Branches.Branch Code values (1,877 rows) plus the 5 Branches.Branch Name values (1,290 rows). Both joins match 100%. The split is at the same row boundary as the other format changes (rows 6-1295 vs 1298-3174). Branch shapes: 'A' 1,877 vs 'Aa Aa'/'Aa' 1,290.
facts.root_cause: (1) profile._semantic only sets codes=True when 60% of the top values look upper-case. It got 5 of 10 with avg_len 6.76, so Branch is not a 'code' column and never gets a codes question. (2) interview.alias_pairs needs a prefix or SequenceMatcher >= 0.88, and 'lnf' vs 'linden falls' fails. (3) profile.find_joins orients the join lookup-to-fact (Branches.Branch Code -> Register.Branch, because a_in_b 1.0 >= b_in_a 0.5). analyze._unmatched_insights then sees rows_matched 1.0 and skips, so '1,290 rows have a Branch not in Branch Code (Linden Falls...)' was never produced. (4) There is no detector for a fact column covered by two columns of the same lookup row. The result is the note 'LNF ... the largest of 10 locations'.
facts.code_refs: sheetbrain/profile.py _semantic() codes rule, find_joins() orientation block; sheetbrain/analyze.py _unmatched_insights() skip on rows_matched>=0.995; sheetbrain/interview.py alias_pairs()
facts.general_fix: When a fact column's values are covered by the union of 2+ columns of one lookup table (code + name, id + label), build the value map from the lookup rows. Canonicalize before any grouping recipe. Write a counted fact ('Branch holds names on N rows and codes on M rows; Branches maps each name to its code') and ask one confirm question. Orient every join toward the unique side, so fact-table values missing from the lookup key always surface as an unmatched finding.

facts.fact: Payroll systems changed with the 04/17/2026 check. On old-system rows Reg Hrs includes overtime, so true regular hours = Reg Hrs - OT Hrs. From 04/17 on, Reg Hrs is regular only.
facts.question: None
facts.data_signal: Four columns switch format at the same boundary. Check Date is 1,290 text 'MM/DD/YYYY' cells vs 1,877 real datetimes (profile shapes '9/9/9' 1290 vs '9-9-9 9:9:9' 1877). Employee Name is 'LAST, FIRST' 1,290 vs 'First Last' 1,877. Branch is names vs codes. Chk/Adv # is 5 digits vs 70xxxx. The last old check is 04/07/2026 and the first new one is 2026-04-17. Arithmetic proof: Gross = (Reg-OT)*Rate + 1.5*OT*Rate fits 213 of 213 old rows with OT and 0 new ones. Gross = Reg*Rate + 1.5*OT*Rate fits 308 of 308 new rows with OT and 0 old ones. Non-RN-FIELD Reg Hrs is above 80 on 176 old rows (every one has OT > 0) and never on new rows (max 80). Without this rule, Harrow Point Jan-Mar regular hours come out 13,897 instead of 13,746.
facts.root_cause: profile.profile_column types a column as 'date' only when 90% of cells are datetime objects. Check Date is 59%, and text dates are never parsed, so Check Date becomes a text 'dimension'. That leaves no check_date role and no date column in the main table. analyze._sign_flips, the only regime detector (and sign-only), returns immediately. Nothing detects format regimes across columns. The payroll playbook runs no hours x rate = gross recipe, and product_check is global, not per regime or OT-aware. So nothing could prompt the owner to mention the switch.
facts.code_refs: sheetbrain/profile.py profile_column() type thresholds (n_date/tot >= 0.9); sheetbrain/analyze.py _sign_flips() (needs c.type=='date'); playbooks/payroll_hr.json insights (no product_check); sheetbrain/recipes.py product_check()
facts.general_fix: (a) Parse text dates in one consistent format before typing a column, and record that the column mixes formats. (b) A shape-regime detector: per row, compute each column's shape family. When 2 or more columns switch family at the same contiguous row or date boundary, write a counted fact ('rows before D look like one export, rows after like another: <columns>'). Then ask: 'Did something change at D? Does any column mean something different before and after?' Use open text plus options. (c) An arithmetic identity search over the main table's numeric columns: C = A*B, C = A*B + k*D*B, C = (A-D)*B + k*D*B for k in {1, 1.5, 2}, scored per regime. When the best identity differs by regime, state it as a counted fact and ask the owner to confirm.

facts.fact: Type V is a void. It is printed positive with the same check number as the check it cancels. Drop both the V row and the original, and keep the M reissue.
facts.question: Round 2: 'What do the codes in Type mean (A, M, R and V)? Type them in your own words.' The pairing rule itself was never asked. The owner added it in free text.
facts.data_signal: Chk/Adv # is unique on 3,139 of 3,167 rows. 14 numbers appear twice, and every pair is exactly one R and one V with the same Emp ID and the same Gross. All 14 V amounts are positive. Each voided employee has an M check about 4 days later (for example E0324: R and V 01/09 $4,729.38, M 01/13 $4,729.38). The tool's own functional_deps computed 'Chk/Adv # -> Type, 14 exceptions', but it went only into an edge record, and edges are not written to the tab.
facts.root_cause: The duplicates recipe runs only on the playbook's employee_id role, not on the table's natural key. FD exceptions are never turned into findings. The meaning came through only because _code_questions offered an open-text box. It is stored as quoted text, and no rule applies it: rules.py has no pair-cancel rule, so top_share and the column sums include voided checks.
facts.code_refs: sheetbrain/recipes.py duplicates(); playbooks/payroll_hr.json insights 'duplicates:employee_id'; sheetbrain/profile.py functional_deps(); sheetbrain/findings.py finding_questions() (no FD-exception branch); sheetbrain/brain.py for_tab() (edges not in tab)
facts.general_fix: Add a near-key finding. When an identifier column is unique on 98% or more of rows, group its duplicates. If each group is one row of code X plus one other row with equal amounts, ask: 'N numbers appear twice, each once as X with the same amount. What does an X row do to its twin?' Offer: cancels both / reverses (net) / separate / not sure. Store the answer as a pairing rule that ctx.rows applies. Also surface any A->B dependency that has a few exceptions as a finding.

facts.fact: E0999 (Jordan Pell) is a test employee the new vendor created. Its checks were never paid. Leave E0999 out of everything.
facts.question: None. Volunteered inside the headcount answer, so the brain scopes it to headcount.
facts.data_signal: The ID E0999 sits far outside the sequence of every other ID (E0101 to E0325, 674 past the max). It has 5 checks (2026-04-17 to 06-12), each exactly $600.00 = 40.00 h x $15.00 with the identical net of $505.68: zero variance across periods. The Employees row shows hire 2026-03-29 (just before the new system's first check), term 2026-06-15, Status T. It appears only in the new-system export. It adds $3,000 to April-June gross.
facts.root_cause: No sentinel or test-record detector exists. E0999 is present in Employees, so the unmatched finder is silent. The leave-out went only into the headcount-framed text, and rules.exclusions ignored it (the _KINDS gate), so count_distinct ('225 distinct employees') and top_share count it.
facts.code_refs: sheetbrain/analyze.py _table_insights() (no sentinel check); sheetbrain/rules.py _KINDS; sheetbrain/recipes.py count_distinct() uses col.distinct, not filtered rows
facts.general_fix: Add a sentinel detector. Flag: an ID that is an outlier in its own sequence (numeric part far above the dense run, repeated 9s or 0s, or tokens like TEST, DUMMY, XXX); an entity whose rows are identical in every metric across 3 or more periods; an entity whose life spans only one regime. Ask 'Is <id> (<n> rows, each exactly <amount>) real, or a test to leave out?' with meta.exclude on the leave-out option.

facts.fact: The bookkeeper stacked two exports, and each part ends with a total row. Total rows must not be counted.
facts.question: None
facts.data_signal: Row 1296 has '*** EXPORT TOTAL ***' in Employee Name, with every ID and date column blank. Its Reg Hrs (77,683.25) and Gross (1,881,321.75) equal exactly the sums of rows 6-1295. Row 3175 'Report Total' equals the sums of rows 1298-3174. The tool's profile shows Gross Pay max 1,881,321.75 and sum $6.38M (true data $4.50M), and Reg Hrs max 77,683.25 against a typical value of 114 or less.
facts.root_cause: tables._TOTAL only matches labels that start with 'total' or word characters. '*** EXPORT TOTAL ***' starts with '*', so the row stays as data. Only 'Report Total' (the trailing row) is caught. analyze._table_insights then asserts 'Register Detail has 1 total or subtotal row inside the data, left out of every count' without checking which row it caught or where. No numeric test (row = sum of the block above) and no outlier check exist.
facts.code_refs: sheetbrain/tables.py _TOTAL regex and _build_table() totals loop; sheetbrain/analyze.py _table_insights() 'structure:totals_rows' statement; sheetbrain/say.py readout() Money line uses col.sum
facts.general_fix: Detect total rows numerically. A row whose identifier and date columns are blank and whose metric cells each equal the sum of the rows since the previous break (to the cent) is a total, whatever its label. Strip non-alphanumerics before the label regex. Flag metric cells 20x or more above the p99 as suspected totals. Write the structure note only from verified facts: how many rows, where, and that they are excluded.

facts.fact: RN-FIELD is paid per visit. On those rows Reg Hrs is visits and Rate is per visit, so visits never go into hours.
facts.question: Round 3: 'What do the codes in Job mean (BR MGR, CNA, HHA, LPN, RN, RN-FIELD and SCHED)? Type them in your own words.'
facts.data_signal: On RN-FIELD rows Reg Hrs is an integer on 339 of 339 R rows (other jobs 32 to 48%). OT is never above 0 (other jobs 67 to 227 rows with OT). Rate is $64 to $82 against $38.25 to $46 for RN. Median 'hours' is 19 against 61 to 78.
facts.root_cause: No unit-heterogeneity detector. It was captured only because an open-text codes question existed. _code_questions emits one column per round (break after 1), so Job reached the last allowed round (MAX_ROUNDS=3). A third coded column would never have been asked. The rule is stored as text only, and the column sums still add visits to hours.
facts.code_refs: sheetbrain/interview.py _code_questions() 'if len(out) >= 1: break', MAX_ROUNDS; sheetbrain/brain.py _column_statement() sums
facts.general_fix: For a quantity column grouped by a category, flag categories whose distribution is a different kind: integer-only while peers are fractional, never paired with a companion column (OT), rate far from peers, median far off. Ask 'On <category> rows, is <column> hours or another unit (visits, units)?' Ask all code columns in one batched question, not one per round.

facts.fact: Type codes: R regular, A adjustment (retro, missed differential, or clawback shown negative), M manual office check.
facts.question: Round 2 Type codes question (same as above).
facts.data_signal: Type is a 4-value code column: R 3,068, A 47, M 38, V 14. Gross Pay has negatives (min -106.31) on A rows.
facts.root_cause: This worked: _code_questions flagged Type (codes=True). One gap: no negatives finding ran, because the payroll playbook lists no negatives:gross_pay insight.

facts.general_fix: Keep it. Add negatives:<additive money role> to every playbook with money roles, so a negative line is always explained.

facts.fact: Payroll is biweekly with checks on Fridays, and manual checks usually go out on a Tuesday. 08/21 is the last August payday, so August is not short.
facts.question: None
facts.data_signal: Regular check dates are every 14 days on Fridays (01/09 ... 04/03, then 2026-04-17 ... 2026-08-21). Off-cycle M checks fall on Tuesdays (01/13, 01/27, 04/07). One judge penalized an answer that called August short.
facts.root_cause: Check Date was typed text, so no date recipe ran on it. No cadence recipe exists. The brain's only date span was Hire Date (2018-01-02 to 2026-08-04), which suggests the data ends 08-04.
facts.code_refs: sheetbrain/profile.py profile_column(); sheetbrain/recipes.py (no cadence recipe); sheetbrain/brain.py Composer._meta()
facts.general_fix: Once event dates are parsed, compute the dominant interval and weekday, plus off-cycle dates. Write a counted fact such as 'checks every 14 days on Fridays; last regular 2026-08-21; N off-cycle checks on other weekdays'. Ask only if the cadence is irregular.

misleading_notes.note: Headcount includes, per the owner: "Not sure about those groups. Leave out the Kestrel Bend (KSB) Amberlane staff and E0999 Jordan Pell (a test employee, not a real person)."
misleading_notes.effect: This is the root of the biggest error, which every model made. Answers applied the exclusion only to headcount and kept KSB in gross, hours and OT. Q1 came out $1,834,105.39 (opus, sonnet) or $1,837,105.39 (luna) instead of $1,537,873.81. Q3 named Kestrel Bend (2,179.5 OT) instead of Linden Falls (412). Several answers read 'Amberlane staff' as an unidentified subset of people at KSB and asked the owner to identify them ('says nothing identifies the Amberlane staff', 'requests employee identification'). Haiku 'limits E0999 and KSB exclusion guidance to headcount'.
misleading_notes.cause: The playbook template 'Headcount includes, per the owner: {answer_labels}' wrapped free text that says the opposite (leave out). rules.exclusions ignored it because headcount_def's kind 'definition' is not in _KINDS. So no exclusion record and no counted 'totals without KSB' note were written, and every counted insight kept KSB and E0999.
misleading_notes.fix: Classify free-text answers by what they say, not by the question they answer. A leave-out sentence becomes an exclusion record with its own neutral statement ('Rows where Branch is KSB or Kestrel Bend, and Emp ID E0999, are left out of all totals, per the owner'), plus the counted with/without totals from _exclusion_facts. Ask one follow-up to confirm the scope.

misleading_notes.note: LNF is 16% of Gross Pay ($738.7k), the largest of 10 locations.
misleading_notes.effect: It confirmed to answering AIs that KSB is a normal branch among many. It split each branch in two: LNF alone is 16%, but LNF plus Linden Falls is $1.27M (28%). Answers built 5-branch summaries with KSB included.
misleading_notes.cause: recipes.top_share groups raw strings, with no name-to-code canonicalization. It ran with no exclusions because rules.exclusions returned {}, and it includes voided checks and E0999.
misleading_notes.fix: Canonicalize groups through the lookup table before any grouping recipe, and apply every owner rule. Suppress a share insight while group identity is unresolved (a column that mixes codes and names).

misleading_notes.note: There are 225 distinct employees in Emp ID.
misleading_notes.effect: This headcount includes the 28 Amberlane staff at KSB and the test employee (our own is 196). Haiku reported headcounts that include KSB.
misleading_notes.cause: recipes.count_distinct reads col.distinct from the whole-column profile. Even with exclusions set it would not re-scope. duplicates, blank_rate and date_range behave the same way.
misleading_notes.fix: Recompute every counted insight from ctx.rows(t) (the rows that remain after owner rules), not from column profile stats.

misleading_notes.note: Header row: 'Written on 2026-09-26, when Register Detail had 3,168 rows, dated 2018-01-02 to 2026-08-04', plus 'Hire Date runs from 2018-01-02 to 2026-08-04 (104 months)'. The Check Date column note was dropped from the reader view.
misleading_notes.effect: The brain never says when checks run. Haiku (both runs) read only the text-dated rows, said the file ends 04/07/2026, and reported April-only gross ($276,836.70 = text-dated April rows exactly). One opus answer called August short.
misleading_notes.cause: Composer._meta takes the first date_range insight in the file, which is the Employees Hire Date, and pairs it with Register Detail's row count. Check Date was typed text (59% datetime), so it had no date_range. Its column note 'Check Date on Register Detail is a category...' was flagged by is_imperative (it starts with 'Check', and the copula is the 6th word), so context_pack left it out. No note says that the column mixes text and real dates. The 3,168 row count also includes the export total row.
misleading_notes.fix: Take the header span only from the main table's own event-date column, after parsing text dates, and omit it when there is none. Add a counted note whenever a column mixes value types or formats, giving the formats, their row counts and where each applies.

misleading_notes.note: Register Detail has 1 total or subtotal row inside the data, left out of every count.
misleading_notes.effect: False reassurance. Readers trusted that totals were clean, and haiku 'does not establish that totals exclude both export total rows'. The row it caught is the trailing Report Total. The one actually inside the data (*** EXPORT TOTAL ***) is counted.
misleading_notes.cause: The tables._TOTAL regex missed the starred label. analyze._table_insights writes the sentence without checking where the caught row sits or whether any other row equals a block sum.
misleading_notes.fix: Detect total rows numerically, and state only what was verified: the count, the row numbers, and whether each is excluded.

misleading_notes.note: Tab baseline rows 'Gross Pay on Register Detail is a number, from -$106 to $1.88M, summing to $6.38M' and 'Reg Hrs ... from 0 to 77,683.25, summing to 261,136'.
misleading_notes.effect: A reader that opened the _brain tab directly (sonnet r2) 'claims an existing _brain tab with incorrect totals'. The owner agent also flagged the $6.38M figure in the readout as possible double counting.
misleading_notes.cause: The export total row is counted as data. The column-statement sums then double the old export, include RN-FIELD visits in hours, and include KSB, E0999 and voided checks.
misleading_notes.fix: Fix totals detection. Leave sums out of baseline column notes, or label them as raw column sums before owner rules and show the rule-applied total next to them.

misleading_notes.note: Owner rules quoted in the tab (Job codes, Type codes) sit inside the workbook file.
misleading_notes.effect: Judges repeatedly penalized answers for attributing the RN-FIELD, void and Amberlane rules to 'the workbook' or 'source-file notes', although the brief says the spreadsheet does not contain them.
misleading_notes.cause: context_pack tags told notes as '[said per owner]' but gives no date or channel. The notes physically live in a tab of the file, so answers cite the file.
misleading_notes.fix: Render each told note as 'Owner, told on <date> (not in the data)', and have the pack header say the notes came from an interview with the owner, not from the sheet's data.

other_defects.defect: A failed save reports success. When write_brain raises BrainError, cmd_save still emits ok:true, 'Done. <file> now has a brain.', next:'build', with written[].result null. It silently ignores --copy (target falls back to the original path), and it logs 'save ... 60 records' to the store log either way.
other_defects.evidence: Owner reports: two saves failed with 'namespace http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/officeDocument/2006/relationships not declared on root', yet returned ok:true, and the out folder stayed empty. The build log.md has 3 'save ... 60 records' lines (11:50:19, 11:50:31, 11:56:06). The first two wrote nothing. The root cause was brainzip._prefix: openpyxl declares xmlns:r on each <sheet>, not on the root. A fallback was added to brainzip.py at 11:54:32, after the run's failures, and the 11:56 save worked. The success-on-failure path in sb.py is unchanged.
other_defects.fix: When the requested destination was not written, emit ok:false (or saved:false with next:'ask'). Name the fallback in the first line of say, and fail loudly when --copy cannot be honored. Log only verified writes. Add a regression fixture whose namespaces are declared per element.

other_defects.defect: The how-to note in the tab is cut mid-sentence.
other_defects.evidence: HOWTO_STATEMENT is 543 characters, and Composer._rec truncates every statement to 500. The tab row ends '...notes that still hold keep their rows '. The same cap would silently cut any owner answer over 500 characters.
other_defects.fix: Never truncate told or meta notes. Split long statements into continuation rows (the tab already has a 'part' column), and add a unit test that every built-in statement fits.

other_defects.defect: is_imperative false positive on computed notes.
other_defects.evidence: 'Check Date on Register Detail is a category, 36 distinct values.' matches IMPERATIVE ('Check'), and _COPULA finds no copula in the first 5 words. context_pack drops it and prints '(1 note that reads like an instruction was left out. It is text in the file, not a direction.)', which suggests to readers that the file carries an injected instruction.
other_defects.fix: Run the imperative lint only on told, inferred and received text. Before testing, strip known column headers from the start of a sentence, or skip template-generated computed notes.

other_defects.defect: The title block was parsed as a table and given a nonsense key.
other_defects.evidence: Rows 1-3 (company name, report title, 'Printed ... User') became 'Register Detail#1' with header 'Quillfield Home Care Staffing, LLC'. The brain states 'Each row on Register Detail is unique by Quillfield Home Care Staffing, LLC.' and 'Register Detail has 3,170 data rows, 2 tables.' The real table has no key note at all: Chk/Adv # is unique except the 14 voids.
other_defects.fix: Treat a one-column band of 5 or fewer text rows above a table as a title. Write key notes only for tables with 2+ columns and a meaningful row count, name the table (not just the sheet), and report near-keys with their exception count.

other_defects.defect: Grill order put a destructive duplicates question before row grain.
other_defects.evidence: At round 0, row_grain had value 12 and find_dupes_employee_id had value 6. next_round alternates finding questions with playbook questions, finding first, so '221 Emp ID values appear more than once... Is that the same one twice? (keep oldest / keep newest / different)' was asked before 'Is each row one person, one paycheck...'. Picking a merge option would have collapsed 3,163 paycheck rows.
other_defects.fix: Always ask grain first, and gate entity-ID duplicate questions on the grain answer. For an event grain (paycheck, shift, order line), drop them and ask about duplicates on the event key instead.

other_defects.defect: No 'Not sure' on 4-option questions, and canned scope options.
other_defects.evidence: interview._options_for adds NOT_SURE only when a question has fewer than 4 options. headcount_def has 4 (part-time, seasonal, 1099, on leave), none drawn from the data, so the owner had to type 'not sure', even though the footer says it is always fine.
other_defects.fix: Always accept not_sure: add it as a parsed text answer, or cap playbook options at 3. Build scope options from the data's actual groups (branches, job codes, Status values).

other_defects.defect: Answer options add words the owner never said.
other_defects.evidence: 'Rows that repeat a Emp ID: different, keep both, per the owner.' comes from the option label 'Different, keep both' ('They only share the value'), but the owner meant 'same person, different paychecks'. The open item restates 'Are they the same ID?' about two name columns. The headcount template put 'Headcount includes' in front of a leave-out sentence.
other_defects.fix: Write the note from the meaning of the choice ('Emp ID repeats because each row is one paycheck'), not the button text. Word mapping questions by column semantics (names: 'same people?'). Never wrap free text in a template whose verb it contradicts.

other_defects.defect: The spread insight uses procurement wording, lowercased codes and nondeterministic examples.
other_defects.evidence: '7 jobs were bought at prices more than 5% apart across locations (for example cna, hha, br mgr)': pay rates are not 'bought'. It compares across 10 'locations' (names and codes), across all months (no date column) and old vs new systems, and it includes per-visit RN-FIELD rates. With no qty, per_item is all zeros, so the examples come from set iteration order: profile.json says 'lpn, rn-field, rn' while the tab says 'cna, hha, br mgr'.
other_defects.fix: Take the verb and nouns from the playbook role ('paid at rates'). Tie-break deterministically (by spread size, then code). Keep the original case, canonicalize groups, and exclude categories whose unit differs.

other_defects.defect: One code question per round and a hard 3-round limit.

facts.fact: F2b: The software changed from Rentquill to Doorvale on 2025-07-01. That is why property names, unit formats, codes and descriptions change mid-year: PMT=PAY, RENT=RNT, LATE=LTF, PARK=PRK, UTIL=WSR, Alder Court=ALDER CT, Dunmore House=DUNMORE HSE, Birchwood Flats=BIRCHWOOD, Cedar Row=CEDAR ROW.

facts.data_signal: The whole vocabulary changes at one date. RENT ends 06-01 and RNT starts 07-01. PMT ends 06-30 and PAY starts 06-01 (the copies) or 07-01. Unit is int on 1,627 rows before July and text on 1,692 from the June DV copies on. Ref # changes from RQ###### to DV-#######. Volumes stay steady across the switch.
facts.root_cause: There is no detector for a vocabulary change at a date. _sign_flips only watches the sign of metric columns. The Unit int/text split was reported only as 'numbers stored as text, so sums skip them'.

diagnose:inventory.business: inventory (Three Herons Restaurant Group: Weekly Counts 5,702 rows, Waste Log 999 rows, Item List 51 rows; build a1). Replayed the question picker from the recorded answers (interview.next_round) against the source workbook: round 1 = goal, find_blank_notes (value 9.0), cost_basis (5.0), find_dupes_item_id (6.0); round 2 = codes_location (1.5, exactly TAU), snapshot, count_unit; after round 2 no candidates were left, so 3 of HARD_CAP 10 slots went unused. All three eval misses trace to code 4 (every model), plus bar /12, P9 and the Aug 16 duplicate for haiku.

facts.fact: Waste reason codes: 1 spoiled or out of date, 2 prep or cooking mistake, 3 dropped or broken, 4 sent back to the vendor (credited, so leave it out of waste dollars), 5 staff meal (counts as waste).
facts.question: None. No question touched Waste Log's Reason Code. The brain only has a baseline node, not shown to readers: 'Reason Code on Waste Log is an ID, from 1 to 5.'
facts.data_signal: Waste Log col G 'Reason Code': 999 rows, 5 distinct integers (1:420, 2:190, 3:155, 4:112, 5:122), 15 stored as text (three of them '4'). No legend anywhere in the workbook. Raw Est. Loss by code: 1 $14,601, 2 $4,637, 3 $13,839, 4 $11,689, 5 $3,131 (total $47,897). With the owner's rules (bar /12, no P9), code 4 is $11,200 of $31,272 (36%), the biggest single code. Notes line up with codes: code 1 = past use-by, slimy, temp alarm; code 2 = overcooked, wrong cut; code 3 = dropped, broken bottle. Codes 4 and 5 have zero notes (0/112, 0/122). The owner's chosen build was exactly waste dollars by kitchen and item. Effect: Ridgeline Jan-Jun $8,257 vs key $5,046, July $3,058 vs key $2,123.
facts.root_cause: No detector could reach it. (1) profile._semantic types an all-integer column whose header contains 'code' as 'identifier'. Col.codes is only set in the text branch, so a numeric code column is never flagged as coded. (2) interview._code_questions scans only analysis.main_table (Weekly Counts) and stops after one code column. (3) detect.detect matches roles only from the main table's playbook (inventory). That playbook has no waste, reason or loss role, so Waste Log (scored procurement 0.385, detection mixed=true) got no roles and no recipes. (4) Picking the build 'waste dollars by kitchen and by item' starts no pass over the columns that build needs. This was not a budget cap: the candidate list was empty after round 2.
facts.code_refs: profile.py _semantic lines 260-267 (numeric id) and 271-275 (codes flag text-only); interview.py _code_questions 320-363 (main_table at 322, break at 361), next_round 451-481; detect.py detect 142-150 (roles from chosen playbook only); playbooks/inventory.json roles (no reason or loss role); analyze.py _table_insights 358-362
facts.general_fix: (1) Type-agnostic code detector on every table. Flag any text or integer column with 2-30 distinct values, repeated heavily (count/distinct >= 10), and no lookup table that explains it (no join to a table with a description column). (2) Rank code questions by the money each code carries (sum of that table's money column per code), and allow one per table. (3) Ask two things: 'What does each code mean?' then a multi-select 'Which of these should NOT count toward <money column> totals?'. Store the second answer as an exclusion rule on (table, column, values) that rules.exclusions applies to recipes. (4) After the build choice, run a scoped pass over the table(s) the build uses (matched by the owner's words or by header words) and ask any unasked code, measure or blank questions there before saving.

facts.fact: P9 is Pier Nine, the owner's sister's separate summer kiosk (June-August) that shares the count app. It is not part of the group: leave P9 out of every group number.
facts.question: R2 Q1 codes_location: 'What do the codes in Location mean (HS, MC, P9, RDG and RL)? Type them in your own words.' Note: 'P9 = Pier Nine, my sister Lucia's summer taco kiosk, her own separate business ... it is not part of Three Herons, leave P9 out of every group number.'
facts.data_signal: Weekly Counts Location=P9: 182 rows, only in weeks ending 2026-06-07 to 2026-08-30 (13 of 38 weeks). It has 14 of 48 items, and every row is counted by 'L. Castellano', who counts nowhere else. Waste Log P9: 47 rows from 2026-06-02 to 2026-08-30, all logged by L. Castellano.
facts.root_cause: The question asked only what the codes mean. It was a generic codes question scored at value 1.5 (risk 2 x reach 0.75), exactly TAU, so it barely made round 2. The exclusion the owner volunteered was never applied to counted notes. rules.exclusions reads free text only from answers of kind exclusion, scope or coverage, and codes_location is 'definition'. It also skips any value shorter than 3 characters (len(first) < 3), so 'P9' can never become a filter. Verified: forcing kind=exclusion still returns {}. So 'There are 5 distinct storages' and 'HS is 40% ... the largest of 5 storages' still count P9. There is no detector for a value that appears in only part of the date range.
facts.code_refs: interview.py value() 422-448, TAU line 20; rules.py _KINDS line 18, kind filter line 39, len(first) < 3 line 54; analyze.py apply_answers 88-113
facts.general_fix: (1) Partial-presence detector: for each grouping column in a table with a date column, flag values whose rows sit in one run covering less than 60% of the date span. Flag harder when the value's people (Counted By, Logged By) or item set don't overlap the others. Ask it as an exclusion question: 'Part of the business, count it / Separate, leave it out of totals / Same as another code'. (2) Parse leave-out sentences from every free-text answer, whatever the question kind. Match exact column values as whole tokens of any length: keep the length guard only for fuzzy matches. (3) Re-run insights after the rules, and show the rule applied in each counted note.

facts.fact: RDG and RL are the same kitchen (Ridgeline). RDG is the old clipboard code before the week ending May 31, 2026, RL from that week on. Combine them for anything about Ridgeline.
facts.question: Same codes_location question. Note: 'RDG = Ridgeline, the old clipboard code used before the week ending May 31, 2026. RL = Ridgeline from that week on; combine RDG and RL for anything about Ridgeline.' The meaning was asked; the combine rule was volunteered.
facts.data_signal: Weekly Counts RDG: 1,008 rows, weeks 2026-01-04 to 05-24. RL: 816 rows, 2026-05-31 to 09-20. The ranges are back to back with no overlap. Both are counted only by 'T. Reyes', and both have the same 48 items. Waste Log: RDG ends 2026-05-24 and RL starts 2026-05-25, both logged only by T. Reyes and M. Lindqvist.
facts.root_cause: No handoff detector. alias_pairs only compares spellings (RDG and RL don't match) and only on the main table. follow_codes (re-coded items) exists only for codes that are missing from a lookup list. Even with the owner's rule in hand, nothing merges two values in recipes: rules.py and Ctx.rows apply only exclusions. So the counted notes still treat RDG and RL as two of '5 storages'.
facts.code_refs: interview.py alias_pairs 370-395, _alias_questions 398-419; findings.py follow_ups 349-418; recipes.py Ctx.rows 78-84 (exclusions only)
facts.general_fix: Handoff detector for any grouping column with a date column: find value pairs where one's last date is within one period of the other's first date, with no overlap and the same people or items (Jaccard >= 0.8). Ask: 'RDG stops after May 24 and RL starts May 31, same counter and items. Same one under a new code?' Store a mapping rule (RDG->RL) and apply it in Ctx.rows, normalizing values before grouping, so counted notes merge them. Also build mappings from free-text 'combine X and Y' or 'X and Y are the same' sentences in any answer.

facts.fact: Bar items (codes 6xxx) are counted in bottles, but Unit Cost is the Keel & Cork case price, 12 bottles per case. Real bottle cost = Unit Cost / 12, so Ext Value and Est. Loss are 12x too high on bar lines.
facts.question: R1 Q3 cost_basis: 'What is Unit Cost? (a Last price paid, b Average cost, c Standard cost)'. This asks the cost method, not what unit the price is for. The owner volunteered the case/bottle fact. Note: 'Unit Cost is, per the owner: "Not sure which cost method. On Bar items ... The real bottle cost is Unit Cost divided by 12, so Ext Value and Est. Loss are 12 times too high on bar lines."'
facts.data_signal: Bar rows (Unit=BTL, vendor Keel & Cork, items named '750ml' or '1L') have Unit Cost $126-$276 per BTL (median $170.40). Every other category and unit has a median of $0.28-$57.87. Bar is 14.1% of Weekly Counts rows but 77.8% of Ext Value. Bar counts use tenths (.1 to .9, 713 of 802 fractional), while every other category uses only .5. Waste Log bar Unit Cost carries the same case prices. With the owner's rule, bar drops to 22.8% of value and Protein (24.2%) is the largest category. 24 items, not 9, make 80% of value.
facts.root_cause: The playbook's cost_basis question asks about cost method only. No detector compares a group's share of value with its share of rows, or checks a price against its unit column. Instead the tool published 'Bar is 78% of Ext Value ($1.64M)' as an insight. It also listed 'Ext Value equals Count times Unit Cost on 100% of rows' as a passed check and as an 'I'm assuming' line in the first card. There is no rule type for dividing a group's prices by a factor, so the counted notes stay 12x high on bar even after the owner's answer.
facts.code_refs: playbooks/inventory.json questions.cost_basis; recipes.py top_share 155-184, pareto 126-152, product_check 187-216; say.py assume block 203-214; analyze.py apply_answers 88-113 (only exclusions and not_items)
facts.general_fix: Unit-mismatch detector: per category or unit group, compare its share of the money column with its share of rows and of quantity. Flag when the value share is more than 3x the row share, or when unit price is more than 5x the median of peers with the same unit. Ask: 'On <group> lines, is <price> for one <unit> as counted, or for a case or pack? How many per pack?' Store a scale rule (group, divisor) and apply it in recipes before any sum. Never show Ext = Count x Cost as proof the price's unit is right. Whenever a unit column exists, also ask the generic 'Is <price> per one <unit>?'

facts.fact: Magnolia's count for the week ending Aug 16, 2026 was uploaded twice. The Monday Aug 17 upload is the real one; ignore the Sunday upload.
facts.question: R1 Q4 find_dupes_item_id: '48 Item Code values appear more than once (5,702 rows). Is that the same one twice?' This was the wrong frame (repeats are expected in a long weekly table); the owner volunteered the real duplicate. Note: 'Rows that repeat a Item Code: "Different, keep both ... The one real duplicate: Magnolia's count for the week ending Aug 16, 2026 is in there twice. The Monday Aug 17 upload is the real count; ignore the Sunday one."'
facts.data_signal: (Week Ending, Location, Item Code) is unique on every row except 48 pairs, all at MC 2026-08-16. That group has 96 rows (every other MC week has 48) and two Submitted times: 2026-08-16 22:41 (48 rows, Ext Value $53,485.14) and 2026-08-17 09:12 (48 rows, $17,010.36).
facts.root_cause: profile.composite_key tries only 1- or 2-column keys and returns [] when none is fully unique. recipes.duplicates counts repeats of item_id alone, which is always true in a weekly table, so the question pointed at the wrong thing. No detector looks for one (period, entity) group with twice the normal rows and two submit times. The note sits under 'Rows that repeat a Item Code' and never names the rows to drop (no timestamp, no row count). The insight '48 Item Code values appear more than once (5,702 rows)' stays even after the owner said to keep both. haiku reported Aug 16 as $109,230 vs $17,032.
facts.code_refs: profile.py composite_key 288-315; recipes.py duplicates 269-282; findings.py duplicates branch 125-138; brain.py _grain_facts 217-230
facts.general_fix: Search keys of up to 3-4 columns (dates, dimensions, IDs) and accept a key unique on at least 99% of rows. Report the exceptions grouped by the key minus the item column, for example: '(2026-08-16, MC) has 96 rows where other weeks have 48, submitted at Aug 16 22:41 and Aug 17 09:12. Keep the later upload, the earlier, or both?' Save the answer as a row filter on the timestamp column that recipes apply, and write the note with that filter. Only ask about duplicates on a column that is actually a key.

facts.fact: A blank count means the item was not counted that week; treat it as zero.
facts.question: None.
facts.data_signal: Count is blank on 15 of 5,702 Weekly Counts rows (0.26%), and Ext Value is blank on the same 15. 11 of them are at Ridgeline (RDG 6, RL 5), 3 at HS, 1 at MC. A judged answer then claimed 'missing counts make Ridgeline inventory understated'.
facts.root_cause: The blank detectors skip sparse blanks in a measure. recipes.blank_rate needs at least 2%, and the inventory playbook runs blank_rate only on par and unit_cost, not on_hand. analyze._blank_groups covers only text dimensions with at least 20 blanks and 10%. The brain carries the blank rate only as 'blank_rate: 0.0026' in a column node that readers never see.
facts.code_refs: recipes.py blank_rate 285-295 (threshold 0.02); playbooks/inventory.json insights list; analyze.py _blank_groups 365-379
facts.general_fix: For the main measure of each table (the metric the goal or build uses), ask whenever any blanks exist, however few: 'Blank <measure> on N rows (mostly at X). Zero / not counted, use the last count / unknown, leave the row out?' Store the answer as a rule, and state it in the brain with the row count and where the blanks cluster.

facts.fact: Weekly Counts is one line per item per kitchen per week (counted Sunday night; week ending = that Sunday, Jan 4 to Sept 20). Waste Log is logged as waste happens.
facts.question: R2 Q2 snapshot: 'Is this a count on one date, or a log of stock moving in and out? (a count on one date, b log of moves, c item list)'. None of the options fit; the owner typed the answer.
facts.data_signal: Week Ending has 38 distinct Sundays. Each kitchen has 48 rows per week (P9 has 14), and (week, location, item) is near-unique, so this is a repeated weekly snapshot.
facts.root_cause: The playbook offers no option for repeated counts. The typed answer is stored but never used: stock-value notes still sum Ext Value across all 38 weekly snapshots ($2.11M total, Bar $1.64M, HS $841.3k), which means nothing for inventory on hand. stock_value is marked additive:true with no period awareness.
facts.code_refs: playbooks/inventory.json questions.snapshot and roles.stock_value (additive true); recipes.py top_share 155-184, pareto 126-152
facts.general_fix: Detect a snapshot panel in code: a date column with few distinct values, where (date, entity, item) is about unique and each date repeats the same item set. Then compute stock or balance metrics on the latest snapshot (or as a per-period average), name the period in every counted note, and offer 'repeated counts over time' as an answer option. Treat stock metrics as non-additive across the period column.

facts.fact: All three kitchens buy through the same vendors at the same price.
facts.question: None. The brain says the opposite: '23 items were bought at prices more than 5% apart across storages (for example 4010, 1010, 3040).'
facts.data_signal: In any given Week Ending, each item has exactly one Unit Cost across all locations (0 item-weeks with different prices). Prices look 'apart' only because they rise over time: 13 items differ within a month and 23 across the year. For example, item 4010 is $3.95 in January and $4.23 in September at every kitchen. The real signal is price creep: the HS produce basket is up 15% from Jan 4 to Sep 20, which matches the owner's 'food cost has crept up'.
facts.root_cause: recipes.spread groups by month only when the playbook maps a temporal role (expiry or count_date). 'Week Ending' isn't in the count_date header list, so jd=None and prices were compared across the whole year. That produced a false cross-kitchen claim and missed the price trend.
facts.code_refs: recipes.py spread 310-371 (temporal role lookup 318-324, month key 340); playbooks/inventory.json roles.count_date headers
facts.general_fix: In spread, group by the table's own period column: any date-typed column, picking the one with the fewest distinct values that still splits rows. Don't rely only on playbook-named roles. If prices are identical across entities within each period, write a price-trend note instead ('prices rose X% from first to last period, the same at every location') and never a cross-entity spread.

facts.fact: Owner goals: bring food cost back under control, see where waste dollars go by kitchen and item, and keep the value sitting on the shelves in check.
facts.question: R1 Q1 goal (a Know what to order, b Free up cash, c Stop shrink and waste); R3 build question. Notes: 'The owner's goal for this data is: free up cash and stop shrink and waste.' and 'The owner asked to build first: Where our waste dollars are going, by kitchen and by item.'
facts.data_signal: Not a data fact. The owner's reply '1bc (waste dollars by kitchen and item, and keeping shelf value in check ...)' carried their own words, but state.json stored goal.text = ''.
facts.root_cause: The goal note is built from option labels, so 'free up cash' (the tool's words) became the owner's goal, and the owner's own phrasing was dropped. The inventory playbook has no waste output, so the build options were 'Dead and overstock (needs one more answer)' (it needs par data the sheet doesn't have) and 'ABC classes', with nothing on waste, and the owner had to type the build.
facts.code_refs: interview.py candidates goal 203-213, _parse_body/_goal_from_text 655-698; brain.py _answer_facts 232-312; playbooks/inventory.json goals and outputs; interview.py build_question 484-506
facts.general_fix: When the owner adds words to a pick, quote their words in the note. Mark option labels as the tool's paraphrase ('picked: Free up cash'). Build options should come from the tables present plus the goal: a log table with a money column and a reason or location column should always offer '<money> by <location>/<item>/<reason>'.

misleading_notes.note: Missing reason-code note, plus insight '869 of 999 rows on Waste Log (87%) have no Notes; the rest are walk-in temp alarm overnight, found at back of reach-in, past use-by, over-ordered for weekend.' and open question 'The owner was not sure: ... What does a blank Notes mean?'
misleading_notes.effect: Every model counted code 4 ($11.2k) as waste. Answers said 'waste reasons are mostly unrecorded', recommended requiring a reason on every entry, and said 'the file doesn't give the reason-code meanings'. Judges: 'Missing free-text notes do not mean managers cannot distinguish waste causes: the reason codes already identify ...'
misleading_notes.cause: analyze._blank_groups treated a free-text Notes column (22 distinct short phrases, so semantic 'dimension') as a grouping column. The finding got weight 3, value 9.0, the top question after the goal. Its options (shared by all / missing / no notes applies) only make sense for a class or department column, so the owner said Not sure and it became an open question. The 'the rest are ...' wording lists 4 of 22 values as if that were all of them.
misleading_notes.fix: Leave note, memo and comment columns (by header words; _NOT_ID_WORDS already lists them) and high-variety free text out of group-blank detection. When a fully filled code column sits next to a sparse notes column, point at the code column instead ('Reason Code is filled on every row; Notes on 13%'). Say 'for example' when listing top values.

misleading_notes.note: 'Bar is 78% of Ext Value ($1.64M), the largest of 7 categories.' and '9 of 48 items account for 80% of Ext Value.'
misleading_notes.effect: haiku ranked bar as the top waste and value category ($16,655 bar waste), said case pricing 'may be masking' bar waste (it inflates it 12x), and reported Aug 16 inventory as $109,230 vs $17,032.
misleading_notes.cause: The counted notes are computed without the owner's /12 rule, since there is no scale-rule mechanism, and summed across 38 weekly snapshots. With the rule, bar is 22.8% of value, Protein is the largest, and 24 items make 80%.
misleading_notes.fix: Re-run recipes after owner rules, including scale rules. When an owner rule covers a note's columns and can't be applied, drop the note or label it ('before the owner's bar /12 rule'). Compute stock metrics per snapshot.

misleading_notes.note: 'Ext Value equals Count times Unit Cost on 100% of rows (0 rows differ).'
misleading_notes.effect: Reads as proof the values are right. sonnet said bar unit costs are unconfirmed and contradicted the owner; judges: 'Says bar unit costs are unconfirmed, which contradicts the owner's knowledge'.
misleading_notes.cause: recipes.product_check reports matching arithmetic as a passed check, and say.py shows it as an 'I'm assuming' line. The arithmetic is exactly why bar values are 12x wrong.
misleading_notes.fix: When an owner note says a column's unit or value is wrong for some rows, mark the check superseded or rewrite it: 'the arithmetic holds, but per the owner Unit Cost on bar lines is per case, so Ext Value there is 12x too high'.

misleading_notes.note: 'Unit Cost is, per the owner: "Not sure which cost method. On Bar items ..."'
misleading_notes.effect: sonnet 'falsely attributes uncertainty about bar pricing to the owner'.
misleading_notes.cause: The question asked about cost method. The owner's 'not sure' about the method and the firm bar rule were saved as one note under one label.
misleading_notes.fix: Split multi-claim free-text answers into one note per sentence or claim, and attach uncertainty only to the sentence it belongs to.

misleading_notes.note: 'HS is 40% of Ext Value ($841.3k), the largest of 5 storages.' and 'There are 5 distinct storages in Location.'
misleading_notes.effect: These contradict the owner (three kitchens, P9 not ours, RDG = RL). Answers compared kitchens on inventory held ('Ridgeline wastes the most for its size'), which judges called unsupported.
misleading_notes.cause: The P9 exclusion was never parsed (kind filter, length < 3 guard), there is no mapping merge for RDG/RL, and the sum runs across 38 weekly snapshots with bar inflated 12x.
misleading_notes.fix: The exclusion, mapping and snapshot fixes above. Also re-derive the entity count from the owner's rules ('3 kitchens after the owner's rules; the column has 5 codes').

misleading_notes.note: '23 items were bought at prices more than 5% apart across storages (for example 4010, 1010, 3040).'
misleading_notes.effect: A false claim that contradicts the owner's 'same vendors at the same price'. It invites a vendor-pricing tangent and hides the real price creep.
misleading_notes.cause: recipes.spread fell back to comparing prices across the whole year because 'Week Ending' isn't a playbook temporal role. At weekly grain, 0 items differ.
misleading_notes.fix: Group by the table's own period column, and report a price trend when prices match across entities within a period.

misleading_notes.note: 'The owner's goal for this data is: free up cash and stop shrink and waste.'
misleading_notes.effect: Judge: 'Attributes a "freeing up cash" goal to the file that the owner never stated'.
misleading_notes.cause: The goal note is filled from option labels (_in_sentence of 'Free up cash'), and the owner's own parenthetical was dropped (goal.text stored as '').
misleading_notes.fix: Quote the owner's words when they add any. Mark labels as the tool's paraphrase.

misleading_notes.note: Insight '48 Item Code values appear more than once (5,702 rows).' plus the duplicate note filed under 'Rows that repeat a Item Code'
misleading_notes.effect: haiku kept Magnolia's Sunday upload: Aug 16 value $109,230 (Magnolia $70,495) vs $17,032.
misleading_notes.cause: The duplicate detector runs on a column that isn't a key. The owner's rule is attached to that frame and never says which rows to drop (MC, 2026-08-16, Submitted 2026-08-16 22:41, 48 rows).
